utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have our witness brought into the courtroom, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we could turn the air conditioning down a bit. Good morning to the interpreters, to the court stenographers, to Defence and Prosecution counsel, and good morning to our witness, General Blaskic. I would like the registrar to tell us where things stand in respect of time used by the Prosecutor for the cross-examination and, most importantly, how much time is left. I don't think he has much time left.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The Prosecutor has, up to now, used 13 days and 270 minutes for the cross-examination, and the Defence in its examination-in-chief had used 14 days and 100 minutes, that is, 150 minutes for the Prosecutor, that is, he still has another 150 minutes, in other words, this morning until about 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kehoe, you have understood that at 1.00, you will be finished. Will you still need some more time? Will you need to do something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would respectfully request, and I realise Your Honours' admonitions prior to this time, but I would respectfully request that you allow me to finish at the end of the day. I do have a few matters to cover which will probably take me another, approximately, three hours at the end of the day. With all due respect, Mr. President and Your Honours, if I could request that additional time until 5.30, I would greatly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you like to make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it will surprise Your Honour -- good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours -- that we object strongly to that request, and on a couple of very basic grounds: Number 1, the Court has made very clearly that there would be equality between the parties with respect to the examination of this crucial witness. If the Court is to have credibility with the parties in terms of finishing this case on time and making the parties to stick to the parameters the Court has set, we urge the Court to stick to those parameters. Secondly, I am shocked that Mr. Kehoe would ask for a doubling of his remaining time, and I wonder how he could possibly have planned his cross-examination in that way, unless he has somehow secretly communicated this request to the Court previously, and I would be shocked if that had occurred. He knew how much time he had left, he's had days and days to budget his time, so I'm sure the Court hasn't received any secret request or secret communication from the Prosecutor indicating that they would seek more time. In light of that, it's hard to understand what the request really is. Number 3, the tactic, by and large, of the Prosecutor in this cross-examination has been to marshal the evidence and argue the evidence. On hundreds of occasions, Mr. Kehoe has read lengthy portions of the transcript, sometimes five, six, seven, eight different witnesses have been read by Mr. Kehoe, portions of the transcript, and the witness at times hasn't been asked to comment at all. Sometimes he's been asked to comment on one or two per cent of what has been read. And what does that mean? That means the Prosecutor, by and large, has used this cross-examination as a mechanism for argument. Therefore, the Defence, in the alternative, we would insist and demand that if any additional time is given to Mr. Kehoe for his cross-examination, the Defence must have that additional time added on to its time for final argument and the Defence have a disproportionate amount of time for final argument because that's the only way balance could be restored to these proceedings. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Hayman overlooks one very crucial fact about his case, and that is his case has gone six days over. He said he was going to be held to 60 days. That was his timetable. He himself went past that time frame by at least six days. It could be more, Mr. Registrar, I'm not exactly sure, but the calculation is it's at least six days. What the Prosecution is asking for is to the end of the afternoon to complete the cross-examination. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We did not exceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, did the Defence use more than its time? Did it go several days longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, we didn't, Mr. President. We did not know how long they would take on cross-examination, and I do not believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I would take the liberty, Mr. Hayman, with all the respect I owe both to you and to the Prosecution, that when I'm speaking to the registrar, perhaps he could tell us, and of course we will give you the floor. I don't know whether the interpreters are following everything that I'm saying here. Did the Defence take more time than was scheduled?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: At the end of the 51st week, that is, last week, according to my calculations, we had 68 days and 240 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you used eight days and 40 minutes longer. So in respect of the rights of the accused, the Judges did not want to say that you had to stop before that. It would have been difficult. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Two issues, Mr. President: Number 1, we did not go over. We didn't know how long they would take on cross-examination. Had they not taken as long on cross as we took on direct, the Defence case would have ended within 60 days. So we do not accept that we went over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. There were 60 days that had been planned for the Defence, and you used 68 days. So according to my calculations, you went over by eight days; otherwise, I don't know how to add. Mr. Registrar, would you clarify things for us? Are we talking about the 60 days that we spent for the cross-examination of the Defence independent or, rather, the entire cross-examination -- all of the days that were used by the Defence to present its case. That's what I think we're talking about. That's what I think those 60 days referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So the question is merely one of knowing whether, beyond the Rules, certain adaptations can be used. If you use eight extra days, that is eight more than 60. That's about a 12-per cent increase. I don't think that the Judges said to you that you had to stop at 60 days. What do you think, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we stopped our direct examination of General Blaskic with, I don't remember how many full-time day equivalents it was, six or ten remaining for the Prosecutor to conduct his cross-examination. We didn't know how many days he would need, and I submit that we made reasonable calculations with respect to the length of direct and cross. The Court participated greatly in direct; that's fine; we welcome it. But what Mr. Kehoe is somehow suggesting is because his cross has gone over the time period allowed for the Defence, he should be given a disproportionate amount of time now as a punitive measure. Because whatever the length of the direct examination of this witness was, the equivalent time period expires at 1.00. So Mr. Kehoe isn't asking for equality of arms; he's asking for inequality of arms. He's asking for an extra half day. If the Court grants that, we want an extra half day in closing argument because the Court surely recognises that a very large bulk of the cross-examination has been argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I would like to consult with my colleagues, but I'd like to set aside the issue of the closing arguments. I have the feeling that, despite what you're saying, the Judges have never stopped you. I don't see myself, I think my memory is good and my colleagues will tell me if I'm wrong, I don't remember having said to you, "Stop. You have to be finished now. You have to stop questioning General Blaskic." I don't think I ever said that. I allowed you to do what you needed to do, and it was during your direct examination that we said to the Prosecutor that you will have the same amount of time, and I was rather strict with the Prosecutor. The problem now is somewhat different. We have to know so that the Judges can be absolutely clear about what they're doing. Do we give the Prosecutor the possibility of concluding his cross-examination, keeping in mind the higher interests of justice? We're working on justice here and trying to ascertain the truth. In any case, I've noted that you have opposed any type of extension, and I will allow the Prosecutor to finish this evening. I first want to consult with my colleagues, and I think that the Judges have spoken a great deal and intervened frequently when they asked their questions. In your right to redirect for General Blaskic, how much time are you going to need, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We expect less than one day equivalent. We're not going to argue the case, we're going to conduct redirect examination, and if they're given any more time -- we don't need it in redirect, we want it in closing argument because they have argued the case through cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with the issue of closing arguments later. Right now, we're talking about the cross-examination of General Blaskic, and I would like to consult with my colleagues. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Nobilo, the Judges will base their decision on Article 90(G) which states that: "90(G) The Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to (i) make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth; and (ii) avoid needless consumption of time." On the basis of this Rule and what was said about the time that the Prosecutor had, that he was not supposed to exceed, that is, the end of the afternoon, and further to Mr. Hayman's comments and further to various factual considerations, including the fact that the direct examination was never limited, the Judges never said that you had to finish on this or that day, and the Defence took all the time it needed to question its witness. Further to the consideration that during the direct examination, the witness, who is the accused, could, in a harmonious fashion, guide and allow himself to be guided in a type of cohesive team which meant that the amount of time wasted or lost was really, really limited; that is, for example, General Blaskic to consult his chronology when he said "I did this at ten after eight, eleven after eight," et cetera. Further to that consideration, it is noteworthy to point out that in the cross-examination, it was more difficult for the witness, who is the accused, to answer immediately when he was asked questions by the Prosecutor. It was frequently necessary for the accused to consult his chronology and that took time, and it was normal for it to take time. The Judges' time, which is the third consideration, that time seems to have been distributed both in the direct examination and in the cross-examination, but it is mostly the time that was taken by the accused and by the Prosecution to look for a certain number of documents. In respect of all these considerations, the Judges note -- and this is the fourth observation -- that the request for additional time is really a marginal one in a trial which has lasted for two years and in respect of the most important thing for the Judges, that is, to find the truth in this complicated and difficult case, and that the time requested by the Prosecutor really isn't very much; we're talking about two or three additional hours this afternoon. Last point. There will be a Status Conference set up, I believe, next week. Judge Shahabuddeen will not be here because he must work in the Appeals Chamber in the Rwanda Tribunal but he has authorised the holding of that Status Conference, and I suggest that at that point, it will be a closed session, that the entire end of the trial be subject to a new schedule that will be arranged by Mr. Fourmy, and the Defence will be able to make its request to be granted additional time to answer the arguments on the merits of the Prosecution. Having made all these considerations, we grant the additional time requested by the Prosecutor, with it being, of course, understood that that time will come to an end at 5.30 this afternoon. The Judges apologise to the Prosecutor who has just lost 30 minutes of his time. Having said this, Mr. Kehoe, you may resume, and Mr. Fourmy will tell you during the Status Conference how the rest of the schedule for this case will be arranged. Thank you. Now we can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You understood that you were asking for additional time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me go back to the question that I asked you yesterday and that we left off on that you were going to find out from your chronology. Did you visit the front lines in Bobasi in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the date, roughly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: September. That's what I asked you yesterday, and you were going to look at your chronology for September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, could I just check this because September --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. The time is short. You can go back and check it at the break. But, Mr. President, at the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We've got to follow the illustration itself. It's natural for General Blaskic to look at his notes, but we also have to say that that takes time. Everything's natural here. If it's natural for him to take time, it is also natural for the Prosecutor to ask the witness to look at his chronology during the break, and you have the right to do so. All right. Continue, please, Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The only problem, Mr. President, is that he doesn't get a break. If he has to work and study and find things in his notes during the break, it's not a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond to that? Yesterday afternoon, I asked the question concerning visiting the Bobasi front line. The witness said, "I have to consult my chronology." And Your Honour broke for the day saying, "Yes, he must consult his chronology and come back with the information tomorrow." Now, that was the same question that I left off on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was not a directive. It wasn't a request by Mr. Kehoe that he look at his chronology overnight and the Court didn't direct him to, and we can pull up the transcript if there is a question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you really are a formidable debater, but I'm also a formidable debater. I don't like specious arguments. I would like this discussion to end now. We have made our decision on the basis of a legal foundation. The Rules give us the power to argue as we have done. I would like to point out that with respect to the breaks, they're always longer, especially when we ask the witness to consult his chronology. It does appear to me that sometimes the witness had a weaker memory when he was looking at his chronology for requests made now than when you made the requests, but since I don't have the same skill as you do, I thought that it was natural because since you are working closely with your client, it was, of course, much easier for Mr. Nobilo when he would say to him, "Today we are going to take up the day of the 17th of April. What did you do?" And your client would look at his chronology. Therefore, please, let's stop this discussion. The Prosecutor has until 5.30 today. If General Blaskic needs to consult his chronology during the break, the Judges are perfectly prepared to give him five additional minutes during the break, and, in fact, everybody will be able to rest, starting with the Presiding Judge and the interpreters. All right, Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during the times that you spent at the front lines, did you see civilians digging trenches at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see civilians digging trench lines at the front line. I was at many front lines. I saw work platoons that were mobilised to prepare shelters, but I did not see civilians digging foxholes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us turn to your meeting of the 9th of May that you had with Claire Podbielski, and during that meeting, where you discussed on page 19244, Ms. Podbielski told you and discussed with you a problem with civilians being taken to do labour, and she stated she had come across the problem of civilians being taken by the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade to do trench-digging. Now, sir, in this conversation that you had with Ms. Podbielski, she told you that Bosnian Muslim civilians were being taken to the front lines to dig trenches by members of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. When you got that information, what did you do with it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said already then to the Red Cross official, Claire Podbielski, that I believe that this is a work platoon because she claimed that she had seen them in Busovaca, in town, when they were going out to work, and I said that I would check this out with the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. I asked for information about this in writing to be sent to me, and indeed I did receive information that the work platoon did go to do work, namely, to prepare the front line communications, shelters, et cetera, and that the work platoon consisted of citizens from Busovaca that were mobilised, in regular terms, by the municipal defence department, and I made Mrs. Claire Podbielski aware of this information at our next meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this conversation that you testified about was on the 9th of May, 1993, according to your testimony. How many times did Claire Podbielski, approximately, how many times did she complain to you that detainees, Bosnian Muslim detainees or Bosnian Muslim prisoners of war, were being taken to the front lines to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: She expressed her point of view that civilians were going, and she thought that these were Bosniak Muslim civilians. I cannot recall how many times, but not many times. I always register such claims that she made, and I always tried to check them out and to give her information about this. My impression was that perhaps she did not understand that these were mobilised citizens who lived in the territory of the municipalities of Busovaca and Vitez and who were mobilised by the civilian authorities as persons who had a work obligation. It's not that we discussed that very much because I recorded each and every conversation of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you said that you investigated the matter and received information back that these workers were part of a work platoon, who sent you this information back? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I can. As regards this specific example, the 9th of May, 1993, I was informed by the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade commander in his extraordinary report, who is called Dusko Grubesic, he said that this was a work platoon, mobilised citizens who were going out to do work and who were mobilised by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did anybody from the International Community tell you that detainees and prisoners were being taken from the Kaonik camp and were being forced to dig trenches? The detainees that I'm talking about are Bosnian Muslim detainees. How many times were you made aware of that by the International Community?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already talked about the district military prison in Kaonik and that it was the first time I heard of this claim in February, and the second time was when I heard about the tragic event concerning the killing of prisoners, and this was on the 11th of February. Then in May, I think this was with Claire Podbielski, at any rate, not too many, but I registered every such claim, and I checked it out and wanted that particular action to be investigated. I also made Mrs. Iris aware of this, and I told her about the results of these checks that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, after your conversation with Ms. Podbielski on the 9th, did you call Mario Cerkez and ask him if he was forcing Bosnian Muslim prisoners, and I'm talking about Bosnian Muslim detainees, forcing Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig trenches? Did you ask him that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After this conversation, if you are referring to May, at practically every meeting I had, and usually these were weekly meetings if there weren't any combat operations with the brigade commanders, I insisted that it was prohibited to use detainees or anyone for digging foxholes and shelters. I thought that it was permissible for regularly mobilised citizens in work platoons to prepare access routes and other things that were needed at the front line because they had work duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So other than your weekly meetings, you never specifically made any direct informational request of Cerkez, the commander of the Viteska Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I received this information, I cannot recall all the details, I would always react by checking it out in respect of such efforts. It was obvious yesterday that I issued specific orders that it was only soldiers who could dig foxholes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Darko Kraljevic and Pasko Ljubicic? Did you ask them directly whether or not any of their troops were forcing Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig trenches? Did you do that after you received this specific information from Claire Podbielski?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not do that because Ms. Claire Podbielski was very specific. She said that she had seen that in Busovaca, and this remark of hers pertained to the town of Busovaca where she saw civilians, and that's what she said. They were moving through town, they were walking through town with various devices for digging, with shovels, et cetera, and she wanted me to check this out. I expressed my surprise when Mrs. Iris, the representative of the Red Cross, told me that this was prohibited, and I remember what was prohibited according to various conventions, and then I told her, I said, "Why do you want me to issue orders about something that is prohibited by law?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk just about another person who had an office in your headquarters, Vlado Santic, who we heard testimony about taking individuals to dig trenches. Now, Vlado Santic at this time was the commander of the Jokeri, was he not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was not. As far as I know, he was the commander of the 1st Active Company of the military police, and he also had other duties within the military police, but I'm not sure that he was the commander of the Jokeri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Vlado Santic? After you received this information from Claire Podbielski, did you go down the hall to see Vlado Santic and say, "Vlado, are any of your troops taking Bosnian Muslim detainees out and forcing them to dig trenches?" Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive such information. Had I received such information, had Claire Podbielski specifically said that this pertained to Vlado Santic, I certainly would have checked this out through his commander, but I do not recall Claire Podbielski telling me about that. I wrote down what she asked me to check. I did not have any contact with Vlado Santic on that matter because Vlado Santic was one of the commanders of the company, and the commander of this unit of the military police was Pasko Ljubicic, just as the commander of the Vitezovi was Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you told us over the past several days and in direct examination that the two Bosnian Muslims that had been killed on the front line in February by two soldiers in the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade had been taken from the Kaonik camp. After you received this information from Claire Podbielski, did you call Zlatko Aleksovski, the commander or the warden of the Kaonik camp, to ask him if Bosnian Muslim detainees were being taken out to dig trenches? Did you do that, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You put that question to me yesterday. I did not receive information in February from Claire Podbielski about the incident that occurred. Claire Podbielski was not head of the regional office of the International Red Cross at the time. At that time, it was Mrs. Iris. When I received information from her, I called my chief of staff and I called the commander --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood my question, and I'll repeat my question. You told us that in February, you had heard from ICRC, Iris, that the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade took these two Muslims out from the Kaonik camp to do trench-digging, and they were subsequently killed. Now, my question for you is: After you received information from Claire Podbielski of ICRC in May about this same brigade being accused of forced trench-digging, did you call the warden of the Kaonik camp, Zlatko Aleksovski, and ask Warden Aleksovski if detainees were being taken out by HVO troops and forced to dig trenches? Did you do that after you received this information from Claire Podbielski in May?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot remember for sure whether I did because Claire Podbielski's information was that she had seen civilians in Busovaca, that they were moving through town. She did not say that these were prisoners of war who were being taken away because this was already May when there were hardly any prisoners of war in the district military prison in Kaonik. Possibly, I did check this out because I know that I issued a warning as to how to react if the prison were attacked. There were quite a few attacks against the district military prison, and these attacks were carried out by various groups, and we agreed with the president of the district military court on how the warden of the district military prison should react and how he should get the military police to protect the prison. Now, whether I made a phone call to Zlatko and when I made a phone call, that, I do not recall. Possibly there were such conversations. But I know that a military policeman was killed on one occasion when he tried to repel an attack against the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zlatko Aleksovski tell you that the Viteska Brigade and the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade were taking detainees out of the prison, Kaonik prison, and forced to dig trenches? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had a meeting with Zlatko. I cannot remember all the details, I'd have to look this up in my chronology, but I do not remember any such specific information that he was complaining about the brigades or the commanders of the brigades taking them away. He did complain about various incidents, provocations, provocations against the security of the prison, and I said that measures should be taken in addition to building an additional fence around the prison so that the prison could be protected --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off, but my time is short. General, this meeting with Claire Podbielski was on the 9th of May, and I would like to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 242, annex O, the interview with Mr. Aleksovski which took place on the 10th of May, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This, Mr. President and Your Honours, is part of the report in evidence, 242, written by Mr. McLeod who was an ECMM investigator, if you will, that came to the area in May to inquire into the Ahmici matters and some other matters. This is an interview of Zlatko Aleksovski. If we could turn to page 2 in that, Mr. Usher, the bottom half of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this item, there is a discussion on the problems in the gaol, and Mr. Aleksovski, at the bottom where it says "5th," discusses this matter with Mr. McLeod, Mr. Charles McLeod: "5th is the kind of work that the prisoners have to do. Because I know that the Geneva Conventions do not allow prisoners to be taken for any work if their lives are in danger. I have been warned about that by the ICRC as well. "But I am not the only one responsible for this, because I just carry out orders. The brigade commanders in Busovaca and Vitez give them. Not that I want to avoid my responsibility. Because I am not the one who releases people to do the work. In order to clear it up, I went with Beatrice of the ICRC to the commander in Busovaca where she protested for the people to be taken to work under such conditions. "She was given the answer I almost completely agree with. We here actually do not have enough people to do the security jobs. Someone had to dig the trenches and it happened that the men to do that were the prisoners." That's grammatically incorrect, but "... it happened that the men to do that were the prisoners." General, how far is Kaonik camp from the Hotel Vitez, approximately?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: About seven or eight kilometres; however, I believe the distance was not the problem. The problem was information or, rather, receiving such information. Because we see that the warden knows about the Geneva Conventions and the brigade commanders knew about the Geneva Conventions because I told them about this in my orders. As for my orders, I said that on the 16th of April, which is quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We don't have a lot of time now. You've answered the question. Let the Prosecutor ask you further questions. You can't plead each time you give an answer; otherwise, you're going to have trouble with your Defence counsel. You understand that. Please answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade and the commander of the Viteska Brigade were both commanders that were your direct subordinates, weren't they? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were my direct subordinates, and they never received such orders from me that they should engage prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was he subordinate or not? Please answer the question, General Blaskic. I don't want to have another discussion with your Defence counsel about questions. You're not giving a specific answer to the question, you take three extra minutes each time, and then we have problems when your Defence counsel says that we don't have enough time. I believe we've had enough of this. Please answer the question, because it was a very simple question: Were the brigade commanders subordinate to General Blaskic or not, "Yes" or "No"? I don't want to have any further discussions with your Defence counsel about those questions. We see what the problem is. You take three extra minutes for every answer that you give. Please answer the questions when they are clear. Repeat the question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the brigade commanders for the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca and in the Viteska Brigade in Vitez, were they your direct subordinates?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you had no knowledge that these commanders were taking prisoners, detainees, Bosnian Muslim detainees, from Kaonik camp and taking them to the front line to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that from time to time I received information from the International Red Cross that there were such cases. When I would receive such information, I would check it out, I would investigate the matter and take appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this criminal conduct on the part of your brigade commanders, were any of your brigade commanders, or any soldiers in those brigades, ever charged with a crime for taking these prisoners out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was the case of the indictment from February 1993, when that group was indicted for taking prisoners to dig trenches and also for killing prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me update the question, General: Were any of the members of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade or the Vitez Brigade charged with a crime for forcing Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig trenches after the 16th of April, 1993, and if they were, could you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the 16th of April -- I do not recall and I do not have the records here whether they were indicted or not, but I already said that if there were such cases, that I would react and take measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 16th of April, were any members of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade or the Viteska Brigade disciplined at your direction for forcing Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that if I would receive such information, then measures would be taken. I do not remember whether there was any information that somebody had forced anyone in this way judging on the basis of what I said in my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus on the continuous complaints before the Busovaca joint commission on this score, and to do that, I refer the Court to the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Morsink -- again, he was a Major when in theatre -- and my colleague, Mr. Harmon, asked the following question at page 9889, line 14: Q I'd like to turn to another topic, and that would be the subject of the use of civilians to perform forced labour, specifically trench-digging. While you were in Central Bosnia, were you aware of this particular practice? A I was given protests, according to -- which said that the Muslims (sic) -- Excuse me. A -- that civilians had been forced to dig trenches. I was given this during the meeting of the joint commission. During the meeting, I was made aware of 15 protests in that respect, 10 to 15, 10 to 15. Q And did both sides complain about this practice? A There were complaints about the HVO soldiers who forced the Muslim soldiers to dig trenches. That's how it always was said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really correct. A The HVO soldiers forced Muslim civilians to dig trenches. The protest came from one side only. Now, General, your representative at these meetings, Franjo Nakic -- was Franjo Nakic. Did he come back and inform you, General, as his superior, that there were continuous complaints being made at the joint commission or joint command that HVO soldiers were forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He informed me about all the matters that were discussed at the joint commission, including the engagement of civilians, that is to say, citizens in carrying out engineering work. The question that is mentioned in Mr. Morsink's testimony is civilians, not prisoners of war. I checked this out and I realised that this was work platoons, that is to say, citizens who were mobilised, not Muslims in a discriminatory fashion but Croats and Muslims and Serbs and the Romany, all citizens were mobilised to do this work. That was the previous practice too according to the law on defence, that the civilian authorities would mobilise persons for carrying out such work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus in on your answer and continue on with Colonel Morsink's testimony on this score. On page 9890, line 9: A There is one case to which I was a witness with HVO soldiers accompanying civilians who were carrying shovels, and who had to dig a hole or to dig trenches. When we asked the question of the local HVO commander in that respect, he felt that he had been a little bit cornered, at least that was the feeling that I had, that he was a bit cornered. He became very aggressive and did not allow me to speak with his soldiers or to the civilians cornered (sic) by the matter -- concerned by the matter. Excuse me. A And this incident was presented to the joint commission subsequently. This happened in May -- I think it was May, I don't quite remember anymore -- it was near Stranje. The military commander had a nickname, Marinac. Continuing on page 9892. Q Colonel Morsink, did you subsequently return to Stranje on the 13th of May with HVO representatives and did you meet with local Muslims who were still residing in that community? A We had a meeting at the Busovaca commission, regular ones, with both parties, and we tried to go on site with them. Q When you went on site to Stranje on the 13th of May, what did the population, the local Muslim population, tell you had occurred to them with respect to trench-digging? A They complained that on several occasions they had been forced to dig trenches. They also complained that many men from that area had been taken prisoner at the county prison and that the remaining men were forced to dig trenches. They were the men who had been taken out of the prison and ordered to dig trenches. While they were digging the trenches, several of them were wounded, some of them even died doing the forced labour. Q Now, at this location in Stranje, was there an HVO representative with you when those complaints were made? A Yes, there were members of the joint commission on both sides. Q Now, you mentioned that there were a large number of complaints made at the local commission and at the joint commissions about civilian forced labour. Were those complaints being made in front of Franjo Nakic? A Mr. (Franjo) Nakic was present several times at various meetings, and he was spoken to. Q Were those complaints also made in front and in the presence of local brigade commanders as well? A Yes. The HVO Busovaca command was always there at that type of meeting. Q Can you tell the Judges what was the response of the HVO in the face of these continuous allegations that civilians were forced to be trench-diggers? A There were different reactions. Sometimes they said furious civilians had forced other civilians to dig the trenches and sometimes we were told that there had been abuses, that some had used HVO uniforms in an inappropriate manner, and on other occasions we were told that the HVO had already lost a great deal of ground and were therefore forced to have recourse to all type of reserve forces and that they had to call upon civilians to dig the trenches, and yet on other times there was no reaction at all. They just didn't answer the allegations. Q Were you also told that it was uncontrolled elements who were forcing civilians to dig trenches? A Yes. That's what they meant when they talked about furious civilians. That's what they meant. Q In addition to complaints that were made to the HVO at the local joint commissions, did other international organisations make complaints to the HVO about this pervasive practice? A The International Red Cross and the UNHCR were present at those types of meetings, and I remember that Margaret Green from the UNHCR had protested because she had noted that there were Gypsies in the Vitez region who had been forced to dig trenches. Q In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, was Colonel Blaskic aware of this illegal practice? A He had to have been because his representatives were present at the meetings and we talked about it. Q To your knowledge, did the HVO ever take any action to stop this illegal practice? A No. I never heard of any kind of measures taken at all. Q Did you ever hear of a single HVO soldier being punished for engaging in this illegal practice? A Never. Q In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, why did the HVO engage in this practice? A I think that it is dangerous work on the front line, and I think that they did not want to put their own soldiers in danger by forcing them to dig this type of trench. So during these meetings, General, that you had with Franjo Nakic, did he tell you, on these continuous complaints by the International Community and by the Bosnian Muslims, that they objected to Bosnian Muslim civilians and detainees being taken to the front-line positions to dig trenches? Did he tell you that, given that he was your chief of staff, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that he informed me about the work of the joint commission, and I'm not a legal man but I believe that if civilians are mobilised in regular fashion who are recruits and conscripts and take part in the work platoons, that that is not against the law. Here, the question of the Gypsies, the Romanies, were mentioned, and I remember the work platoon was called Svace, and each village had its work platoon made up of civilians and they were mobilised by the civilian authorities and they had their salaries and were entitled to sick leave and everything else, pensions and so on. Today they enjoy the right to shares and to have their years of service. So these civilians were mobilised within the composition of the work platoons but not for the elaboration of shelters, communications, access roads, and they were called general purpose units within the general system of civil defence and they were mobilised by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you said in this courtroom and you heard testimony from -- I can't give you a number -- many Bosnian Muslims who were taken to the front lines and forced to dig trenches and they testified to soldiers -- excuse me, of Bosnian Muslims being killed at those front lines and wounded. Now, how many Bosnian Muslim detainees or civilians were killed and wounded on the front line while they were digging trenches or any type of fortifications for the HVO? How many, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the number for sure, how many there were, but I do know that whenever I received any information, I reacted to it and launched an investigation into the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, after the 16th of April, did you ever launch and react to information of a Bosnian Muslim detainee or civilian who had been shot or killed on the front line and did you gather information as to the circumstances of that individual being shot or killed on the front line? And if you did, when did you do it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember one particular case -- I don't remember all the details of the case -- but I think it was the Vitez Brigade, after the 16th of April, a civilian died, a Bosniak Muslim, and I received a report from the security service about that. I think that a company commander was suspected of being to blame and an inspector of the company also was killed. So I remember that one particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what happened to that company commander, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was also killed, I think on the 19th or 18th of April, but up until the 20th of April, he died too -- he was killed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that example, you have no other information in that area, do you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned that example because I remembered it. I think his name was Slavko, the company commander's name was Slavko, and I've already said, if the information reached me, I quite certainly did react and demanded an investigation into the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us, in this conversation that you had with Claire Podbielski where you found out about these civilians being taken out to dig trenches, you told us that you subsequently found out that this was part of a work platoon. Now, General, if a work platoon had been sent to a front line position, a dangerous front line position, to dig trenches, based on your training in the JNA and training in the Geneva Conventions, would such a practice be unlawful?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, if they were taken to dangerous positions. But I've already said that my orders were very precise, that a soldier must dig his own foxhole, and it was standard practice in the JNA, and this can be seen from a Defence Exhibit, I don't know the number exactly, but military positions are established throughout the year, and from September 1992, for example, there is a document where I order that the territory be prepared for defence, so it is implied that a soldier dig his own foxhole, and work platoons in the JNA dug shelters, access trenches, put roads right, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you ever order that work platoons consisting of civilians be sent to the front lines to engage in trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall having issued orders in that sense. And may I explain, please, briefly? A platoon is mobilised by the civilian authorities, according to their own criteria, and it is made up of all citizens that have this work duty, and the local commander, the commander of a position comes to collect these men and engages them in organising accesses but not foxholes. I keep receiving the translation of "tranceje," an interpretation of communicating trenches. That is different. That is where the army relaxes, sleeps. So there's a big difference between "foxhole" and "shelter."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you direct work platoons to where they should go to dig trenches or foxholes? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't remember directing work platoons as to where they should go. I would issue orders to the commanders of brigades, issue military orders, but I don't recall I myself giving orders as to where a work platoon would go. Work platoons went where the local commanders at the municipality level or local community level wanted them to go. Each village in the municipality had its own work platoons. They had their civilians. Every village had this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the civilians who had been sent to the front lines to dig trenches, were any civilians killed at the front-line positions while they were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did not dig at the front line. In military terminology, there is a basic front line and an auxiliary front line. They did not dig trenches at the front line or the auxiliary front line. They dug shelters and accesses to shelters, and I can draw a diagram of this as to how I understand this, these facilities. This is essentially different. Perhaps there were. I said beforehand that this whole enclave was a battalion in defence, that a whole battalion could be placed there, but it was all a dangerous region and was within rifle range, not only artillery range. Perhaps there were some people who were wounded, but if such cases occurred, they would have equal rights, just as soldiers did, to a retirement pension, to benefits, their years of service would be recognised, just as any other soldier belonging to the HVO had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, General. We'll just deal with civilians who were part of these work platoons. Were civilians who were part of these work platoons killed at the front line; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know whether anybody, any of them died at the front line because, as I have already said, they were mobilised by the civilian authorities, and I had no influence on the work of those civilian authorities nor competence over them. It was the head of the defence department who had his own criteria, and he assigns to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Answer the question, General Blaskic. Answer the question, please. The question is whether there were people killed on the front line. Either you know or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps there were. I do not have any precise data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us move on. Were you given information or did you come by information or were you informed that these civilians who were part of these work platoons were wounded at front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I usually received operative reports and numerical data, for example, three soldiers or ten soldiers today, in the course of the day, from the Vitez Brigade, or ten members, were wounded, for example, whereas the work platoons were within the composition part of the civil defence, and they sent their data to the commander of the units, general purpose units of the civil defence organisation. That was what usually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how about abuse of civilians who were parts of these work platoons? Did you receive information that HVO soldiers were physically abusing these civilians who were part of these work platoons?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving information about any abuse. I would certainly have reacted, and if a soldier did that, then that was at the level of a company or a battalion or brigade, for measures to be undertaken. But I received collective information about disciplinary measures. For example, in September, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade had ten disciplinary measures and punishment taken towards soldiers. Now, whether within those cases, there were cases of this kind, I don't know, but I have, for example, the figure of 60, that 60 disciplinary measures were taken for that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go into another area. I don't know if you want to take a break now. It would be a more convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to take a 20-minute break. I would like the accused, who is a witness, if he needs a little more time, if he needs to do some research into the subject, he can. So I suggest that we take 25 minutes, Mr. Hayman, so that would give the client the time to do some research if he needs the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, if there's a particular assignment. I don't know if there's a particular standing request for him to look through his notes during this break or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There was no request, no specific request. Do you need to do any research? Do you need to look something up, General Blaskic, something short.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I need about five minutes, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did have a specific request of the witness that I had at the outset, and that specific request was the initial question, was there a front-line position at Bobasi in September and did he visit it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You had all evening to think about it, but perhaps in the next five minutes, you will get the answer. All right. We will take a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Mr. Hayman, I hope it will be noted in the transcript that your client had 32 minutes to look through his chronology. Mr. Kehoe, you can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in September of 1993, was Bobasi a front-line position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the front line passed through Bobasi, but I did not tour that part of the front line in September 1993, so I did not walk and tour it on foot from trench to trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've given them to the registrar, Mr. President. The next three documents, Mr. President, that we are discussing are all seized documents, documents that were seized pursuant to a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document is 715, Prosecution Exhibit 715 and 715A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do the booths have the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do have some extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then put them on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the first document is a document dated the 10th of September, 1993. General, this document is dated two days after the attack in Grbavica was completed. This is a report from the defence department signed by Marijan Skopljak and the report on the organisation of work platoons of the Vitez HVO, and a copy of it is delivered to the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, that is, to you. We will not read this entire document, but the first three paragraphs are instructive on page 1: "Pursuant to the Decree on the Establishment of the Armed Forces of the HZ HB /Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna/, the Temporary Regulations on the Mobilisation of the Armed Forces of the HZ HB and instructions on keeping military records on v/o /conscripts/, and in connection with the newly arisen situation in Vitez municipality, as of 16 April 1993, the Defence Office activated the work platoons set up so far and assigned them to work on engineering consolidation and organising the first defence lines. "Work platoons (units) whose mobilisation was carried out by the Vitez Municipality Defence Office partly consists of Croats in the category of persons unfit for military service, and the remaining part comprises of Romanies or Muslims. "The Sofa and Zilic Work Platoons were established as units attached to the Defence Office on the first day of hostilities. The members of these platoons are Romanies. Use of these platoons falls under the authority of the Vitez Defence Office. We would immediately like to mention that these work platoons have carried out 80% of the jobs related to the engineering arrangement of territory for the entire municipality of Vitez. The total number of people in both platoons amounts to 55 members (45 in the Sofa and 10 in the Zilic Work Platoons). We consider it necessary to mention that both work platoons have not had a single day off during this war and have conducted their jobs mainly in night-time conditions and quite often while under enemy fire. Two members of the work unit were killed while at work and two were wounded. Both work platoons received work unit identity cards and a wartime station, the prescribed form." Let us move to the last page of the English version, which is the second to last page in the B/C/S version. For you, General, it's at the bottom of the page, and it begins: "On 8 September," the 8th of September being the date that the Grbavica attack ended. "On 8 September 1993, a verbal order was issued by Colonel Blaskic to engage a minimum of 100 people from the work units to work on the consolidation and digging-in on the first defence lines on the Jardol-Divjak-Grbavica axis towards Sadovace. The Defence Office embarked on the mobilisation of its work unit, and the first group was sent to the Vitez post office at 1600 hours exactly. The total number of people sent on behalf of the Defence Office and the Viteska Brigade was 83 members because Stipo Zigonjic of the Defence Office went to the location in Sector Bila, activated the work platoons of Stara Bila and assigned a number of people to load sacks in Pjescara and the remaining personnel to dig in at the first defence line. The total number of men was 40. "The total number of people mobilised for the digging of trenches in the Grbavica-Divjak-Jardol area amounts to 123 v/o [conscripts] which can be confirmed by Mr. Dragan Grabovac, the chief of the Viteska Brigade engineering. "It must be said that, according to the people in the work units, there were problems regarding the execution of the above-mentioned tasks. When the men arrived, one group was immediately put to work and another group was received promptly but not put to work immediately; it only started working at 2400 hours because the work was badly organised. Some members of the second group were abused and beaten by some soldiers, which can be established on the basis of statements of the commander of the work unit." Now, General, you told us you never sent civilians in these work platoons to front-line positions to dig trenches. This report from Mario Skopljak reflects somewhat differently, when on the day the Grbavica attack ends, on your verbal orders, a minimum of 100 people from work units were to go to the Jardol-Divjak axis to dig-in on the first defence lines. So when you told us that you didn't order platoons to go to the front-line positions, that wasn't true, was it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I did not issue direct orders to the work platoons, but in my testimony, I refer on the 7th of September -- I referred on the 7th of September, I testified that I had a meeting at about 1630 with the mayor of the municipality of Vitez, the head of the defence department, Mr. Marijan Skopljak, a representative of the regional civilian police, and the chief of staff and the chief of engineers, and we then discussed the topic of the consolidation of Grbavica once the position had been taken over. Once again, it was the soldiers who held the front line and who had taken over Grbavica and taken up their positions whereas on Grbavica itself, shelters were being built and accesses. So in this part of my testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're not going to repeat the same things, General Blaskic. I would like us to go straight to the matter at hand. I had not understood that you had given a verbal order on the 8th of September, an order to engage a hundred people for the work platoon. That's what we've got to focus on. You never said that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, not on the 8th of September, but on the 7th of September, at a meeting which was a meeting of the civilian and military authorities, I expressed myself on the basis -- I expressed a request on the 7th of September at 1630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, General, you ordered these work platoons to go to dig on the first defence line which is on the front line of the HVO, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said, at the front line we had soldiers of the HVO holding the front line itself. I expressed the demand, vis-à-vis the defence department, to mobilise the work platoons. I did not order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was it a false order? Let me remind you that you're under oath. You're not in a civil law system here. You are a sworn witness. Let me remind you of that. Is this document a false document which does not express the truth? That's the question which is being asked. You are not in a civil law system where you testify freely without taking an oath which means that you have the right to lie. You do not have the right to lie before this Tribunal once you've taken an oath at the request of your Defence counsel. That's what has to be said. Let me repeat the question to you: Is this document a false one and does not express the truth? Please shed some light on that question for us. It is your right to answer.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document in its contents expresses the truth except for the fact that I, on the 8th of September, issued an order. On the 7th of September, I expressed my demand to the defence department at the meeting attended by five or six other people. So I expressed this demand at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I have noted your answer as it was given. That's much more appropriate in respect of the legal system in which all of us practice. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in this order that you received from Mr. Skopljak, the order in the last paragraph notes that: "Some members of the second group were abused and beaten by some soldiers." Now, General, what did you do when you received this information that HVO soldiers were beating members of the civilian work platoons?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I specifically do not remember all the measures undertaken, but I can see in this document that it speaks about the statements of the commander of the work platoons, and I do believe that certain steps were taken connected to the investigation, but I really cannot remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you give us one name of one soldier, HVO soldier, who was prosecuted and convicted or disciplined as a result of beating civilians in the work platoons? One name, General. And the time frame that I'm talking about is in September of 1993 when you received this document from Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember the name and details related to this document, the names of soldiers who were punished on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us turn to the next two documents, if we could, and we will take these two in tandem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are Exhibits 716, 716A, 717, and they're all Prosecution Exhibits. The "A" refers to the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if the witness can be given 715 as well? I would like him to have all three exhibits with him. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we've got 717 and 718 before us -- excuse me, 716 and 717. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- 716, if we can put that on the ELMO? Is that 716? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 716 is the order or the report of the 21st of September, 1993, again by Mr. Skopljak, and his report was submitted to your headquarters, General: "Based on a verbal request made by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and in connection with the mobilisation of personnel / work platoons for conducting work on engineering consolidation of the Bobaseva Kuce defence line, we inform you of the following: "The Vitez Municipality ... has mobilised 20 people, the Sofa Work Platoon, (the mobilisation was carried out by the Defence Office ... Stipo Zigonjic and Marijan Vinac) consisting of the following." Now, General, take a look at the 20 individuals from the Sofa work platoon who were taken to this Bobaseva Kuce defence line. All of those individuals are Muslims, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the work platoon -- I think -- I think they were Romanies, but they could be Muslims too. I'm just talking about their names now, because the defence department mobilised the work platoons, that is to say, the civilian authorities, according to their own criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, 1 through 20 in that group, they are all Muslim names, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm looking at document 717. Perhaps I'm not looking at the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to object to the question. It is not precise enough. In Bosnia, there are different ethnic groups, the Bosniaks and the Romanies, and being Muslim is a faith, and both the Romany and the Bosniaks belong to that religious group. So could you please tell us whether the question relates to an ethnic or religious group because it's an important distinction?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I am referring to the 20 names on the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to the 20 names on the report of 21 September, 1993, which I believe is Exhibit 716, is it not, and those 20 names, as part of the Sofa Works, they are Muslims, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that, to my knowledge, the work platoon Sofa consisted of Romanies. Perhaps there are Bosniak Muslims too in this list, but as far as I know, these were Romanies, the Sofa work platoon. I'm talking about the village. I wish to mention one more thing, that the mobilisation was carried out by the defence department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the Bobaseva-Kuce line was a front line position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Bobaseva-Kuce have their first front line starting from the house of Ivica Bobas and it goes along the houses in the Bobasi villages, but then there were also houses that were adjusted for people to stay at and also to have the front line there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to Prosecution Exhibit 717, and before we go there, General, this particular line in Bobaseva Kuce, that was a practice front line position on the 21st of September, 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is difficult to say now for an entire month what the criteria are for active and what the criteria are for passive. First it would be active and then it would be completely passive because the most active lines in September were to the south of Zabrdze towards the explosives factory, for example. So the most active line was facing the explosives factory from Zabrdze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look at Exhibit 717 which talks about another verbal request by you. This is on the 20th of September, 1993. Again, it is a document that is from Mr. Skopljak from the defence department, a report is sent to you at the Central Bosnian operative command: "In accordance with a verbal request from (Central Bosnian Operative Zone) Commander Tihomir Blaskic and with regard to the new situation in Vitez municipality, the Defence Office has mobilised/activated work platoons. One hundred people were required for engineering consolidation and organisation of the defence line in the Kruscica-Bobasi area." And it lists a group of individuals, 17, from the Sofa work platoon. Now, again, these 17 names are Muslim names, as part of the Sofa work platoon, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I said that the Sofa work platoon consisted of Romanies. Perhaps they are Muslim by faith but they are Romanies, to the best of my knowledge, based on the knowledge I have from the municipality or village, and I know that every village had its own work platoon, and Sofa consisted of Romanies primarily. I heard about "consolidation" in the interpretation that I heard, that 100 persons were required for consolidating the front line. In the document that I have here before me, it says differently. The word "consolidation" is not there. And this document was sent to the defence office in Travnik. It was sent to me, but it was sent to the immediately superior office --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General -- General, on the 20th of September, the Kruscica-Bobasi area was an active front-line position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the criteria applied in the case of active positions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you're a military man. When you talk about an active position, tell me what you think; what you, as a military commander, when you ordered or asked for a hundred people to go to this line, did you consider it to be an active line, General, or why else would you ask these people to go up there to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I did not order these people because it is quite clear from the document that I sent a request to the defence office, that is to say, the institution that is in charge of carrying out mobilisation, setting up platoons, and sending them to that area, Bobasi-Kruscica, to carry out engineering work in order to consolidate the area for the front line. I cannot recall precisely now, when you say September, whether this was an active line. It is my understanding that that would mean that there was fighting there all the time, ongoing fighting, all the time, and that is not the way it was in September, throughout the month of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, so if I understand you correctly, you asked for a hundred people from the work platoon to go dig trenches in the Kruscica-Bobasi area, but you don't know whether or not this is an active front line; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, that is not what I'm asserting. I am asserting that I asked them to go and to consolidate the positions for defence. Give me a date from September and I'm going to tell you exactly whether there was fighting at that front line or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you've got an exact date. It's the first document from Mr. Skopljak, 8 September. An order was given by Colonel Blaskic. I would just like to know: Was the order given or not? It wasn't given? If it wasn't, that's your right to say so. Was it or was it not given? You're under oath, General Blaskic, let me remind you once again.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am aware of that, but I wish to clarify this, Mr. President. The request was given on the 7th of September at the meeting at 1630 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is no request here. This is an order dated 8 September from Skopljak which is sent to the defence organs. It says that an order was given by General Blaskic. Was Skopljak lying or you lying? That's a very clear question. Let's stop it. Let's try to move proceedings forward. Did you give an order or did you not? You've got the right to say "No." But you do not have the right to lie because there is false testimony as well. Either you say "Yes" or you say "No." That's all.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not give an order, I gave a request, that is to say, I requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then that's your answer. Mr. Kehoe, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're going to change subjects at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to talk to you about some of your testimony concerning communications. Now, you told us, from the time that you came to Central Bosnia and became the commander until the time you left, you had fighting against the Bosnian Serb army. Now, during those fights with the Bosnian Serb army, did you have communication abilities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Communication abilities? To communicate with who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your troops, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had the ability to communicate in the Lasva pocket with my troops. In the Lasva pocket, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you communicate with Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, through packet link and also civilian telephones, just ordinary telephones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had your troops on the front lines in Jajce, did you communicate with them, and how did you do it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did it in the following way: I stayed there at the front line in Jajce, most often at certain defence sectors, together with the commander, and from time to time, I had an ordinary telephone, an ordinary telephone which worked every now and then and a packet link which also worked only every now and then. This was August 1992 and also September and October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me move to the first document, General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 718, 718A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could also use that in conjunction with this, if we could hand that out and I'll give you the next document as well and we could talk about it together, it might expedite matters. This is the next document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 719, 719A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, the first document, Exhibit 718, is a document that comes from the main staff in Mostar, dated 21 January, 1993, and it talks about the protection of the operation of packet radio transmitters. In number 3, it notes that: "The Chief of Communications of the Vitez Central Bosnia Operative Zone will submit the detailed report asked for in this document." Now, who was your chief of communications for the Central Bosnian Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The chief of communications for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was Boris Pindek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was his office?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Hotel Vitez. During this period of time, that is to say, the 21st of January, 1993, he was in the Hotel Vitez, and he shared an office with another officer. I can't remember exactly who that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was his office on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this same place, in the Hotel Vitez. He shared an office with another officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me turn to the next exhibit, which is Prosecution Exhibit 719, which is an order by you dated the 23rd of January, 1993, and it is directed to the communications company commander. Now, is that individual to whom you direct this order, among others, different from your chief of communications or is that one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, this is not the same person. This is a different person who was subordinated to the chief of communications. The chief of communications is a professional person working in headquarters, and this is a different person. Zeljko Blaz, I think his name was. I'm sure that Blaz was his last name, but I'm not sure about his first name, whether it was Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many individuals did you have working underneath the chief of communications, in addition to this company commander? An estimate; you don't have to be specific.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know how many persons there were because he was in charge of establishing these units, depending on the equipment that was coming in, and he was commander of a company that was being established, that is to say, that as the equipment arrived, that's how he set up this unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Approximately. The Prosecutor is asking for an approximate number. If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
